This is a scratch page (verso), almost blank. It carries no derivation, only a few symbols and a small pencil sketch.

(1) Top row, four separate symbols: a script capital M (possibly with a flourish), Q, a two-letter symbol read as 'MD' (uncertain), and the angle expression A - P - p.

(2) Below, centred: the product Q sin(A - P - p).

(3) A pencil sketch. It shows a nearly vertical line labelled h, a second line slanting from upper left to the bottom, and a short horizontal base line. A letter g is at the top. A letter that looks like g or f sits at the bottom where the lines meet.

(4) An isolated 'S' on the left margin.

Reading (my interpretation, not stated on the page): Q sin(A - P - p) is the standard form of the component of a force, or a torque, of size Q acting at angle A - P - p to some reference direction. Here A is an azimuth or direction angle, P is a fixed offset (for example a rest position or declination), and p is a small deflection.

That fits the Göttingen setting of 1853, when Riemann was close to Weber's magnetic and electrodynamic measurements:
- M could be a magnetic moment.
- Q could be a directing force (for example the horizontal intensity times a moment).
- 'MD' could be a product of moment and a force constant.
- The torque on a suspended needle or bifilar magnetometer then has the form Q sin(A - P - p).

The sketch, a near-vertical line h beside a slanted line meeting a horizontal base, could be a suspension thread, plumb line, or small-angle deflection figure.

None of this is developed on the page. Nothing is computed, so there is nothing to reconstruct beyond noting the expression. Any identification of the physical problem is conjecture.
